title: Kidneys, nephrons and urine formation
blurb: Name every structure urine and filtrate pass through, in order, locate the parts of the kidney and nephron, and say what filtration, reabsorption and secretion do in each segment.
question: A urinalysis shows protein and red blood cells in a patient's urine. Which part of the nephron has most likely been damaged, and why should those components normally stay in the blood?

teach.body: Formally, the urinary system consists of two kidneys, which form urine, two ureters, the urinary bladder and the urethra, which transport, store and eliminate it. In plain English: the kidneys clean the blood and make urine; everything after them is plumbing and a storage tank. The working unit inside each kidney is the nephron, and there are about 1 million of them per kidney.

teach.caption: Ureters run kidney to bladder; the urethra runs bladder to outside. Urination is called micturition.
Note there are two ureters, one from each kidney, but only one urethra leaving the bladder.
Transitional epithelium (urothelium) stretches as the bladder fills. The male urethra also carries semen.

children.label: Hilum
children.sub: artery in; vein and ureter out

teach.caption: The right kidney sits slightly lower because the liver lies above it. An adrenal gland sits on top of each kidney.

teach.body: Each nephron has a renal corpuscle, where blood is filtered, and a renal tubule, where the filtrate is processed. The renal corpuscle is the glomerulus (a tuft of capillaries) plus the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule that cups it. The tubule then runs through the proximal convoluted tubule, the nephron loop (loop of Henle) and the distal convoluted tubule before draining into a collecting duct shared by many nephrons.

teach.body: Formally, urine forms by glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion: excreted = filtered minus reabsorbed plus secreted. Filtration: blood pressure pushes water and small solutes into the capsule; blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood. Reabsorption returns filtrate to the blood, mostly in the PCT (about 65% of Na⁺ and water, normally all glucose and amino acids); the loop's countercurrent builds a salty medulla; the DCT and collecting duct fine-tune under aldosterone and ADH. Secretion moves H⁺, K⁺, creatinine and drugs from blood into filtrate.

Aaliyah, 22, asks why she keeps getting urinary tract infections when her brother never has. The answer is anatomy. Her urethra is about 4 cm long; a male urethra is about 20 cm. Bacteria have a much shorter trip from the outside to her bladder. The ureters, which run from each kidney to the bladder, are a different pair of tubes and are similar in both sexes.

teach.text: URETERS (two) go kidney to bladder; the URETHRA (one) goes bladder to outside. The AFFERENT arteriole enters the glomerulus and the EFFERENT one exits. The glomerulus is part of the renal corpuscle, not the tubule. MOST reabsorption is in the PCT, not the collecting duct; SECRETION runs blood to filtrate.

items: Urine path: kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra.
Kidney regions: cortex (outer), medulla with pyramids, renal pelvis; hilum for vessels and ureter.
Nephron = renal corpuscle (glomerulus + capsule) + tubule (PCT, loop, DCT) draining to a collecting duct.
Afferent arteriole in, efferent arteriole out of the glomerulus.
Filtration at the corpuscle; PCT reabsorbs the most; aldosterone (DCT) and ADH (collecting duct) fine-tune; secretion adds H⁺, K⁺, drugs.
Bladder: transitional epithelium; internal sphincter involuntary (smooth), external voluntary (skeletal).

summary: You can now trace urine from kidney to outside, label the cortex, medulla and pelvis, and follow both filtrate and blood through the nephron in order, saying where filtration, reabsorption and secretion happen. You can also tell ureters from the urethra and afferent from efferent arterioles under exam pressure.

A.q: Which structures carry urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder?
A.why: The two ureters carry urine from each renal pelvis down to the bladder by peristalsis.

whyNot.1: The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside.
whyNot.2: Collecting ducts are inside the kidney; they drain into the calyces, not the bladder.
whyNot.3: Renal veins carry filtered blood away from the kidneys, not urine.

A.q: Which part of the nephron reabsorbs the largest share of filtered sodium and water, and normally all filtered glucose?
A.why: The PCT does the bulk of reabsorption: about 65% of filtered Na⁺ and water, plus all filtered glucose and amino acids normally.

whyNot.0: The DCT fine-tunes Na⁺ and K⁺ under aldosterone; it handles a small share.
whyNot.2: The collecting duct adjusts water under ADH; it is not the main reabsorption site.
whyNot.3: The ascending limb pumps out Na⁺ and Cl⁻ but is impermeable to water and does not reclaim glucose.

A.q: Which vessel carries blood INTO the glomerulus?
A.why: The afferent arteriole arrives at the glomerulus; the efferent arteriole exits it.

whyNot.0: The efferent arteriole carries blood away from the glomerulus.
whyNot.1: Peritubular capillaries surround the tubule after blood has left the glomerulus.
whyNot.3: The renal vein carries blood out of the whole kidney.

B.q: Which sequence correctly traces filtrate through a nephron?
options: Capsule, DCT, nephron loop, PCT, collecting duct
Capsule, PCT, DCT, nephron loop, collecting duct
Capsule, nephron loop, PCT, DCT, collecting duct
Capsule, PCT, nephron loop, DCT, collecting duct
B.why: Filtrate passes from the glomerular capsule to the proximal convoluted tubule, the nephron loop, the distal convoluted tubule and then the collecting duct.

whyNot.0: The proximal tubule comes first after the capsule; the distal tubule comes after the loop.
whyNot.1: The nephron loop lies between the PCT and the DCT, not after the DCT.
whyNot.2: The PCT comes before the nephron loop; 'proximal' means nearest the capsule.

B.q: Tubular secretion moves substances in which direction, and which is a typical example?
B.why: Secretion moves substances from the peritubular blood into the filtrate; H⁺, K⁺, creatinine and many drugs are secreted.

whyNot.0: Filtrate to blood is reabsorption, the opposite direction.
whyNot.1: Glucose is filtered and then reabsorbed in the PCT; it is not secreted.
whyNot.3: Creatinine is secreted into the filtrate, and filtrate to blood is the direction of reabsorption.

B.q: Which region of the kidney contains the renal pyramids?
B.why: The renal medulla is made up of renal pyramids, which contain nephron loops and collecting ducts.

whyNot.0: The cortex is the outer region holding renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules.
whyNot.2: The renal pelvis is the funnel that collects urine from the calyces.
whyNot.3: Major calyces collect urine from the minor calyces and drain into the pelvis.

C.q: Aldosterone and ADH both act on the late nephron. Which pairing of hormone and effect is correct?
options: ADH: the PCT reabsorbs all filtered glucose
Aldosterone: DCT reabsorbs Na⁺, secretes K⁺
ADH: the DCT secretes Na⁺ and reabsorbs K⁺
C.why: Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb Na⁺ (water follows) and secrete K⁺. ADH inserts aquaporins in the collecting duct so more water returns to the blood.

whyNot.0: Glucose reabsorption in the PCT needs no hormone; ADH acts on water in the collecting duct.
whyNot.2: Adding aquaporins to the collecting duct is ADH's action, not aldosterone's.
whyNot.3: This reverses aldosterone's ion handling and gives it to the wrong hormone; ADH controls water.

C.q: A patient's urine contains large amounts of protein and red blood cells. Which structure is most likely damaged?
C.why: Blood cells and large plasma proteins are normally too big to pass the glomerular filter, so finding them in urine points to glomerular damage.

whyNot.0: The collecting duct adjusts water reabsorption; it does not decide what is filtered.
whyNot.1: The nephron loop builds the medullary gradient; filtration happens before the loop.
whyNot.2: The DCT fine-tunes ion reabsorption; it cannot let cells into the filtrate.

C.q: Which statement about the bladder and urethra is CORRECT?
options: The external urethral sphincter is skeletal and voluntary
The internal urethral sphincter is skeletal and voluntary
The bladder is lined by simple squamous epithelium
The detrusor muscle of the bladder is skeletal muscle
C.why: The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control; the internal sphincter is smooth and involuntary.

whyNot.1: The internal urethral sphincter is smooth muscle and involuntary.
whyNot.2: The bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), which stretches.

reteach.title: A recycling plant with a sieve
reteach.question: Picture a recycling plant: everything small is washed through a sieve, workers pull back the valuables, and the rest goes down a pipe to a holding tank. Which part is which?

blocks.body: The glomerulus is the sieve: water and small items wash through into the capsule, but big items (blood cells, large proteins) are held back. The tubule is the sorting belt: workers in the PCT grab back almost everything useful, and later stations fine-tune. The collecting ducts feed the calyces and pelvis, the ureters are the pipes, the bladder is the holding tank and the urethra is the drain to the outside.

blocks.text: If big items turn up in the waste, the sieve is broken: protein or blood in urine suggests glomerular damage, not a tubule problem.

explain.body: Kidneys form urine. Two ureters carry it to the bladder by peristalsis. The bladder stores it, stretching thanks to transitional epithelium. The urethra carries it out, guarded by an internal (smooth, involuntary) and an external (skeletal, voluntary) sphincter.

test.q: Urine passes through which structure immediately after leaving the urinary bladder?
test.why: The urethra drains the bladder to the outside.

whyNot.0: The ureters deliver urine to the bladder; they come before it.
whyNot.2: The renal pelvis is inside the kidney, at the start of the ureter.
whyNot.3: Collecting ducts are inside the kidney, well before the bladder.

explain.body: Bean-shaped and retroperitoneal. The outer cortex holds renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules; the medulla holds the renal pyramids with loops and collecting ducts; the renal pelvis funnels urine from the calyces into the ureter. At the hilum the renal artery enters and the renal vein and ureter leave.

test.q: Which structure leaves the kidney at the hilum along with the renal vein?
test.why: The renal vein and the ureter both leave at the hilum; the renal artery enters there.

whyNot.1: The renal artery passes through the hilum but enters the kidney rather than leaving it.
whyNot.2: The urethra starts at the bladder, not the kidney.
whyNot.3: Afferent arterioles are tiny vessels inside the kidney that feed each glomerulus.

explain.body: Filtrate collects in the glomerular capsule, then passes through the PCT, the descending and ascending limbs of the nephron loop, and the DCT. Many nephrons drain into each collecting duct, which empties into a minor calyx.

test.q: Which part of the nephron does filtrate enter first?
test.why: Filtrate is pushed out of the glomerulus into the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule, the start of the nephron's tubular path.

whyNot.0: The PCT receives filtrate from the capsule, so it comes second.
whyNot.1: The nephron loop follows the PCT.
whyNot.3: The collecting duct is after the DCT and is shared by many nephrons.

explain.body: Blood arrives in the afferent arteriole, is filtered in the glomerulus, leaves in the efferent arteriole, and then flows through the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta around the tubule before draining toward the renal vein.

test.q: Blood that has just been filtered in the glomerulus leaves it through which vessel?
test.why: The efferent arteriole carries blood out of the glomerulus toward the peritubular capillaries.

whyNot.0: The afferent arteriole brings blood into the glomerulus.
whyNot.1: The renal vein drains the whole kidney, after the peritubular capillaries.
whyNot.2: The renal artery supplies the kidney before blood reaches any glomerulus.
